It's not as noob a question as you think; you're only looking at half the information about the particular calibers you mention.

It's a combination of barrel length, and case capacity. You say 9mm, but all that means is the caliber in question fires a projectile that is 9mm in diameter. The common handgun caliber, 9mm Luger is 9x19. 19 is the case length, to which gives you an idea of how much powder is behind the round... But you might be referring to 9x39 cause the VSS Vintorez is badass. 7.62 is the same story however 7.62x39 is what an AK47 shoots, and 7.62x51 is a common hunting round, and military battle rifle cartridge. 7.62x25 is an old Russian pistol caliber for reference. In general pistol rounds are slower, shorter and kill you by poking a hole in something important so you bleed out. Rifles kill you by dumping a ton of energy into you, and causing your tissue to shred itself getting out of the way. Speed kills. For example. Let's take a 9x19 and a 7.62x51 both firing a 8gram bullet. The 9mm bullet with be traveling at around 350m/s with 490 joules. The 7.62, will be traveling around 940m/s with 3610joules. Getting shot isnt good, but the rifle bullets speed is what makes it exponentially more lethal, and powerful. The gun comes into play with letting the bullet accelerate up to those speeds. A 9x19 fired down a longer barrel, will be faster, and more lethal. A 7.62x51 fired out of barrel half as long as usual will be much slower, and less effective.

Revolvers and shotguns fire much heavier projectiles, much slower than a rifle, but the extra inertia and energy helps them damage the target more like a rifle would, but more due to the direct damage of the hole poke. Ballistic gelatin testing videos can demonstrate this well. Personal opinion, the rifle will always win.

The caliber, let's take 5.56x45 as an example is usually designed for a specific barrel length. 556 was intended for a 20inch barrel, so it would stay supersonic out past 600yards. It's part of the reason that m16s have a 20inch barrel. Once you start cutting the barrel shorter, the bullet has less time to get spin stabilized by the rifling, and more importantly: accelerate. You can make the barrel longer, and the reverse holds true, until you hit the point of diminishing returns, or it's detrimental. Video games do a poor job demonstrating this. The caliber sets the standard of how effective the cartridge should be, the rifle shifts that performance up or down a bit. A 556 bolt action rifle will only be marginally more effective than an M16 if the barrel lengths are identical. Rifles mostly have different ergonomics or accuracy potential.

Calibers are a bit obnoxious and there is no universal naming system. I tend to stick with the metric forms just cause I think it makes more sense; it usually includes the case length. 5.56x45 is also known as 556 NATO, or .223remington here in the US. As corny as it sounds, the YouTube gun community is a great information source. Iraqveteran8888 has tons of explanatory stuff for beginners, and InRangeTv is great. The military arms channel is a classic, and Forgotten weapons is great for learning firearm history. Nssf has some good resources too!

5.56mm is NOT the same as .223 Remington. The various cartridge types may look very similar, or even identical, but the MIL-SPEC 5.56mm chamber is shaped differently, mostly to accommodate varying shapes and types of bullets, and is also tested to higher pressures than your typical .223 Remington. Some 5.56mm cartridges could be outright dangerous in a rifle chambered for .223 Remington.

They're within tolerance of each other, and functionally interchangeable, just like 308 and 7.62x51, Saami and the military measure pressure differently so comparing between the two isn't really possible. If you want to stick to the philosophy of the military chamber is the only one safe for both, go ahead; I don't and the industry really doesn't.
